This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI automation with multimodal LLMs. The core proposal combines three ingredients: hierarchical planning with retrieval from web knowledge and two forms of memory, continual self-updating of those memories via self-evaluation, and an Agent-Computer Interface that exposes a language-centric, bounded action space grounded through an accessibility tree plus screenshot. Empirically, the paper reports a substantial improvement over the OSWorld baseline and additional gains on WindowsAgentArena without explicit adaptation. Overall, I found the paper timely, ambitious, and practically relevant. It addresses an important problem—general computer-use agents—and the system design is coherent. The empirical gains on OSWorld are meaningful enough that the work deserves serious attention.

The strongest aspect of the paper is that it tackles a genuinely difficult setting: open-ended desktop interaction across heterogeneous applications, long horizons, and dynamic interfaces. The proposed decomposition into manager/worker/self-evaluator is sensible, and the distinction between narrative memory for high-level task summaries and episodic memory for subtask-level execution is intuitively appealing. The ACI component is also well motivated. In this domain, grounding and action granularity are major bottlenecks, and the paper makes a convincing case that accessibility-tree-centric interaction with bounded primitives is a better fit for current MLLM agents than raw coordinate prediction or unconstrained code generation. The reported OSWorld improvement from 11.21% to 20.58% is substantial in absolute terms for such a hard benchmark, and the cross-OS transfer result is encouraging.

That said, the paper is more compelling as a systems paper than as a clean scientific study, and several methodological issues limit how strongly one can attribute the gains to the claimed ideas. My main concern is disentanglement of contributions. Agent S changes many things at once relative to the baseline: planning structure, retrieval sources, memory design, self-evaluation, action abstraction, grounding representation, OCR augmentation, and likely prompting. The ablations help, but they are still not fully isolating the effects. In particular, the ACI seems to differ from the baseline not only in action-space design but also in the observation representation and grounding mechanism. Since grounding is known to dominate performance in GUI agents, it is difficult to tell whether the gains primarily come from better planning/memory or from a stronger interface layer. The paper argues both, but the evidence is not yet sufficiently controlled.

A second major concern is the learning/evaluation protocol around memory construction and continual update. The paper emphasizes “self-supervised exploration” and “continual memory update,” including learning during inference. This raises important questions about evaluation fairness and possible contamination. It is not fully clear whether the agent updates memory while traversing the benchmark test set and then benefits on later test tasks. If so, the reported test performance is not strictly comparable to a static baseline, because the agent is effectively adapting online to the benchmark distribution. Even if no exact task repeats, this still changes the evaluation setting from standard held-out generalization to sequential adaptation. Similarly, the initial memory is built from “randomly curated tasks” generated using applications and initial environments from OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena. The paper says environment-aware tasks are generated from initial benchmark environments; this could leak benchmark-specific structure into memory construction. I do not think this invalidates the work, but it absolutely needs much clearer accounting. A top-tier conference paper should specify whether any test-task initial states, applications, or benchmark-specific templates are used during exploration, and should report results with frozen memory versus online-updated memory.

Relatedly, the self-evaluator is underspecified and potentially fragile. The paper states that success/failure is evaluated without human feedback or ground truth information, but does not explain how reliable this evaluation is, especially for partial completion or subtle semantic errors. Since only successful subtasks are stored in episodic memory, evaluator precision matters a lot: false positives could poison memory, while false negatives could suppress useful experience. The ablation “without self-evaluator” suggests summarization helps, but it does not reveal whether the evaluator is actually accurate. A quantitative analysis of evaluator agreement with benchmark success labels, or at least a manual audit of stored memories, would strengthen the claims considerably.

The empirical section is promising but still somewhat thin for the breadth of the claims. The main benchmark result is strong, but the ablation study is conducted on only 65 sampled tasks. Given the high variance typical in agentic evaluation, this subset may not be sufficient to support fine-grained conclusions such as the relative importance of web knowledge versus narrative versus episodic memory. Confidence intervals or repeated runs are absent throughout. Since many of the reported differences in ablations are modest, statistical uncertainty matters. The paper would be stronger with multiple seeds or repeated evaluations on at least the ablation subset, plus uncertainty estimates. Even if API-based models make this expensive, some accounting of variance is needed.

I also found some ambiguity in the comparison setup. On OSWorld, the baseline appears to be the benchmark’s reported agent using screenshot plus accessibility tree and coordinate actions, while Agent S uses a different ACI with element IDs and OCR-augmented tree. This is a reasonable comparison from an engineering perspective, but it is not apples-to-apples if the claim is specifically about hierarchical experiential planning. On WindowsAgentArena, the comparison is to NAVI under a “similar configuration,” but again the exact parity is unclear. Since the paper’s headline claim is state of the art, the evaluation section should more explicitly separate “full system versus prior end-to-end agents” from “controlled component comparisons under matched interface/backbone settings.”

There are also some conceptual overclaims. The paper repeatedly frames the memory update process as analogous to hierarchical reinforcement learning, but there is no reward optimization in the usual sense, no policy improvement guarantee, and no environment-derived scalar reward. This analogy is fine as intuition, but the wording occasionally suggests a stronger connection than is warranted. Similarly, “learning during inference” is an interesting capability, but it should be described carefully as retrieval-memory accumulation rather than learning in the conventional statistical sense.

On the positive side, the error analysis is useful and refreshingly candid. It is informative that execution and grounding errors dominate, and that many execution failures are downstream of planning or grounding mistakes. This supports the paper’s motivation for ACI and hierarchical decomposition. However, the taxonomy could be made more rigorous. The categories overlap substantially, and the paper itself notes causal dependence between them. It would help to report primary failure causes or a causal chain analysis rather than only per-task incidence rates where multiple labels can co-occur.

The paper is generally well written and easy to follow for a systems paper, though there are some presentation issues. A few tables and figure references are inconsistent or awkwardly integrated. Some notation is introduced but not used rigorously. There are also minor signs of haste in the references and appendix organization, including duplicated citations for AutoGuide and some formatting inconsistencies. None of these are fatal, but they do detract from polish.

In terms of novelty, I would characterize the contribution as a strong integration and adaptation of several known ideas rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic principle. Hierarchical planning, retrieval augmentation, episodic/narrative memory, reflection, accessibility-tree grounding, and bounded action spaces all have precedents. The novelty lies in how these are combined for desktop GUI control, plus the specific distinction between narrative and episodic memories and the ACI design choices. That level of novelty is acceptable if the empirical validation is strong and the methodology is careful. Here, the empirical gains are indeed notable, but the evaluation protocol needs to be clarified to fully justify the strength of the claims.

The most important revisions I would request are the following. First, clearly define the evaluation protocol for memory: what is built before test time, what is updated during test time, whether task order matters, and whether any benchmark initial states are used in exploration. Report frozen-memory and no-online-update results on the full benchmark if possible. Second, provide stronger controlled ablations isolating ACI from planning/memory, ideally under the same observation and action interface. Third, add uncertainty estimates or repeated runs for the ablation subset and, if feasible, for the main result. Fourth, analyze the self-evaluator quality, since it is central to the continual memory story. Fifth, discuss computational cost: web search latency, token usage, average steps, and wall-clock time. The conclusion acknowledges this omission, but it is important enough that at least basic numbers should be included now, especially because hierarchical retrieval-heavy agents may trade accuracy for substantial latency.

I also think the paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of safety and robustness. The ACI is motivated partly by safety, but the evaluation focuses only on success rate. In real computer-use settings, bounded primitives and one-action-at-a-time execution may reduce catastrophic errors, but they may also still permit harmful actions. Even a brief discussion of safeguards, failure containment, or sandbox assumptions would improve the paper.

My overall assessment is positive but not unreserved. This is an impactful and practically important piece of work with strong benchmark gains and a thoughtful system design. However, the current version leaves too many questions about evaluation fairness, contribution isolation, and online adaptation to fully support its strongest claims. If those issues are clarified, this could be a valuable contribution to the emerging literature on generalist GUI agents.

I would lean toward acceptance if the venue values ambitious systems papers and benchmark progress, but with the expectation that the authors address the methodological concerns above. If the bar is primarily for clean causal evidence and tightly controlled experimentation, then the paper is somewhat short of that standard in its current form.

Strengths include the importance of the problem, a coherent and well-motivated architecture, substantial gains on a difficult benchmark, useful cross-OS evidence, and a practical interface design that likely has value beyond this specific system. Weaknesses include insufficiently controlled attribution of gains, unclear memory/evaluation protocol with possible benchmark adaptation effects, limited statistical rigor in ablations, and under-specification of the self-evaluator and computational tradeoffs.

In summary, this is a strong systems contribution with real empirical progress, but it needs sharper experimental hygiene and clearer protocol disclosure to match the strength of its claims.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper presents Agent S, an open framework for autonomous GUI-based computer control using multimodal LLMs. The core design combines: (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning, where a manager decomposes tasks into subtasks using online web knowledge and retrieved narrative memory; (2) worker-level execution aided by episodic memory and trajectory reflection; and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that uses screenshots plus an augmented accessibility tree and constrains actions to a discrete set of GUI primitives. On OSWorld, the method improves over the reported GPT-4o baseline from 11.21% to 20.58% success rate, and it also improves over a comparable setup on WindowsAgentArena. The paper includes ablations for web knowledge, narrative/episodic memory, ACI, and memory construction/update components, along with qualitative examples and error analysis.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: general-purpose GUI agents for real computer environments.
The proposed system design is coherent and practically motivated, combining planning, retrieval, memory, and interface abstraction in a unified framework.
The ACI contribution is well motivated: accessibility-tree grounding plus bounded primitive actions is a sensible design choice for current MLLM agents.
Empirical gains on OSWorld are substantial relative to the reported baseline, and the method appears to improve across multiple task categories.
The paper includes several useful ablations and an error analysis, which helps identify where gains come from and where failures remain.
Cross-benchmark evaluation on WindowsAgentArena strengthens the claim that the framework is not narrowly overfit to a single environment.
The work is open-source, which increases reproducibility potential and practical impact.
weaknesses: The overall success rate remains low (20.58% on OSWorld), so despite relative gains the absolute capability is still limited.

The evaluation relies heavily on comparisons to reported baselines under somewhat different agent designs, and fairness of comparison is not fully established, especially when external web search and memory are introduced.
Ablations are conducted on a small sampled subset of 65 tasks rather than the full benchmark, which weakens confidence in component-level conclusions.

The continual memory update setup risks contamination between evaluation instances unless task ordering, memory reset policy, and leakage controls are very carefully specified; the paper does not make this sufficiently rigorous.

The self-supervised exploration tasks are derived from benchmark applications and initial environments, raising concerns that the memory may encode benchmark-specific priors and reduce the strength of zero-shot/generalization claims.

The paper repeatedly frames the method as learning, even analogizing to hierarchical reinforcement learning, but there is no principled learning objective, no policy optimization, and no formal analysis of when retrieval-based updates help or hurt.
Statistical uncertainty is absent: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run variance are reported despite stochastic LLM-based evaluation.

Some presentation details are inconsistent or sloppy (e.g., duplicated references, notation inconsistencies, occasional mismatch between text and tables), which reduces confidence in experimental rigor.
methodological_flaws: Potential evaluation leakage/confounding from continual memory update during inference: if memories are updated while processing benchmark tasks, later tasks may benefit from earlier benchmark interactions. The paper does not clearly specify whether evaluation is single-pass online, randomized, reset between runs, or protected against benchmark contamination. This is a serious empirical validity concern.

The initial memory construction uses synthetic tasks generated from the applications used in OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, and environment-aware tasks are generated from benchmark initial states. This may inject benchmark-specific information into memory, weakening claims of generalization and making the setup closer to benchmark-adapted precomputation than pure zero-shot evaluation.

The claim that the process 'mirrors a classic Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning process' is scientifically loose. There is no reward function grounded in environment success, no optimization over returns, and no policy/value learning. Textual summaries stored in retrieval memory are not equivalent to RL updates, so the analogy overstates the methodological connection.

The self-evaluator determines success/failure and summarizes trajectories without human feedback or ground truth, but the paper does not validate evaluator accuracy. If the evaluator is noisy, memory quality may be corrupted; this central mechanism is not independently assessed.

Ablation conclusions may be unstable because they are based on only 65 sampled tasks, with very small counts in some categories (e.g., OS has 6 tasks). Large percentage swings on such small denominators are not statistically reliable.

No variance across multiple runs/seeds is reported, despite stochasticity from LLM inference, retrieval, and web search. Single-run success rates are insufficient to support strong claims of superiority.
The use of online web search introduces an uncontrolled external information source whose availability/content may vary over time, reducing reproducibility and making exact comparison difficult.

The paper does not adequately disentangle which gains come from stronger grounding/action abstraction versus additional external knowledge and memory. Although there are ablations, the comparisons are not always on the full benchmark and some settings differ in multiple factors at once.

There are notation and formulation inconsistencies in the mathematical description (e.g., switching between E_nu, M_n(Q), K_web/K_ext, reward notation r vs R, and informal equations that are definitions rather than formal derivations). While not fatal, this weakens the claimed formal clarity.
